## 1. Introduction 

Ancient DNA^[DNA recovered from human remains, such as bones or teeth, dating to the past.] has transformed the study of third-millennium BCE mobility^[Here, *mobility* means the movement of individuals or populations between regions.] because it can test whether changes in ancestry accompanied archaeological transitions across Eurasia. Genome-wide ancestry estimates^[Estimates based on DNA markers across the whole genome that indicate which earlier populations contributed to a person’s ancestry.], identity-by-descent segments^[Stretches of DNA shared by people because they inherited them from a relatively recent common ancestor.], kinship^[Biological relationships among individuals, such as parent–child or siblings.], uniparental markers^[Genetic markers inherited through only one parental line: mitochondrial DNA through the maternal line and the Y chromosome through the paternal line.] and isotope data^[Chemical signatures in teeth or bones that can provide clues about where a person grew up or what they ate.] can reveal population relationships and help distinguish long-distance movement from local continuity. These methods are particularly relevant to the Yamnaya horizon^[A widely distributed Early Bronze Age archaeological phenomenon associated with pastoral communities of the Pontic–Caspian Steppe.], whose expansion began near the start of the project’s 3300–2600 BCE interval and was followed by major demographic changes both west and east of the Pontic–Caspian Steppe^[The grassland region north of the Black Sea and Caspian Sea.]. The evidence reviewed here supports a broad model of rapid, bidirectional dispersal^[Movement in two directions—westward into Europe and eastward into Inner Asia.] of Yamnaya-related populations after a multi-stage formation process, followed by regionally variable admixture^[The genetic mixing of previously separated populations.] and restructuring rather than a single uniform replacement event [@allentoft_population_2015; @haak_massive_2015; @lazaridis_genetic_2025; @wang_genomic_2021].

The inferential limits^[The boundaries on what the evidence can reasonably demonstrate.] of this evidence are equally important. Ancient genomes directly record biological relationships and modelled ancestry^[An estimate of ancestry produced by comparing ancient genomes with selected reference populations.], not ethnicity, archaeological identity or spoken language. Genetic results can therefore establish that a population moved, mixed or was replaced, while the connection of those processes to Indo-European language dispersal remains an interdisciplinary interpretation. Archaeological context and historical linguistics^[The study of how languages change over time and how different languages are historically related.] are required to assess whether a demographic expansion also transmitted language. Accordingly, this review distinguishes direct genetic observations from demographic interpretation and then from linguistic inference. It uses calibrated language^[Carefully qualified wording that reflects the strength and limits of the available evidence.] such as “compatible with” or “consistent with” rather than claiming that DNA proves which language an individual spoke [@haak_massive_2015; @tassi_genome_2017; @wang_genomic_2021].

## 2. Evidence for Yamnaya population movement across Eurasia

### 2.1 Formation followed by expansion

Evidence immediately preceding 3300 BCE suggests that Yamnaya ancestry did not arise from an isolated or genetically uniform source. @lazaridis_genetic_2025 modelled a multi-stage process in which Caucasus–Lower Volga-related ancestry moved west and mixed with Dnipro–Don hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, producing most of the ancestry later found in sampled Yamnaya individuals. Their reconstruction places the formation of a core population before the archaeological expansion and the rapid dispersal after approximately 3300 BCE. @nikitin_genomic_2025 provide a complementary North Pontic sequence: Caucasus–Lower Volga-related migrants mixed with Trypillian farmers^[Farming communities associated with the Cucuteni–Trypillia archaeological culture of eastern Europe.] in the formation of Usatove groups, while a parallel mixture with local foragers^[People who obtained food mainly through hunting, fishing and gathering rather than farming.] contributed to Serednii Stih populations, from which later Yamnaya groups derived substantial ancestry. @chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022, using admixture-date estimates^[Statistical estimates of approximately when two previously distinct populations began mixing.] across Europe and western Asia, likewise place important Steppe-ancestry formation processes before the archaeological appearance of the Yamnaya and Afanasievo horizons^[The Afanasievo horizon was an Early Bronze Age archaeological phenomenon in the Altai and nearby parts of Inner Asia.]. These models converge on staged formation followed by expansion, although they do not yet resolve one precise formation centre or every intervening route.

Earlier southeastern European evidence provides necessary context but should not be treated as direct evidence for the 3300–2600 BCE migration itself. @mathieson_genomic_2018 identified intermittent genetic contact between Steppe and southeastern European populations long before the large third-millennium BCE ancestry shifts. This longer history indicates that the Yamnaya expansion emerged from existing networks of contact rather than initiating east–west interaction. However, the rapidity and scale of the later dispersal distinguish it from these earlier contacts. The chronological distinction is therefore between earlier interaction that contributed to ancestry formation, the Yamnaya expansion beginning around 3300 BCE, and subsequent regional transformations within and after the target interval [@chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022; @lazaridis_genetic_2025; @mathieson_genomic_2018; @nikitin_genomic_2025].

### 2.2 Westward movement into Europe

The strongest evidence for Yamnaya-related migration is the large ancestry shift in central and northern Europe near 3000 BCE. @haak_massive_2015 estimated that sampled German Corded Ware^[An archaeological phenomenon of third-millennium BCE Europe named after the cord impressions used to decorate pottery.] individuals derived approximately three-quarters of their ancestry from a Yamnaya-related source, a result inconsistent with an explanation based only on the circulation of artefacts or ideas. @allentoft_population_2015 independently found substantial genetic affinity^[Genetic similarity that suggests shared ancestry or historical population connections.] between Yamnaya and Corded Ware groups across their broader Eurasian dataset. More recently, @ringbauer_accurate_2024 identified long identity-by-descent segments linking several Corded Ware and Yamnaya groups. Because such long segments indicate relatively recent shared ancestors, these results narrow the demographic connection to only a few hundred years and strengthen the case for rapid movement from the Steppe into central and northern Europe [@allentoft_population_2015; @haak_massive_2015; @ringbauer_accurate_2024].

This convergence does not mean that every Corded Ware community descended directly from one sampled Yamnaya population. @haak_massive_2015 acknowledged that their Samara Yamnaya sample might not be the precise source, while @ringbauer_accurate_2024 identified both recent Yamnaya connections and substantial ancestry related to Globular Amphora populations. @papac_dynamic_2021 similarly found that Corded Ware groups in Bohemia possessed high but heterogeneous Steppe-related ancestry that could not be explained entirely by the sampled Yamnaya sources. “Yamnaya-related ancestry” is therefore more accurate than assuming descent from a single homogeneous Yamnaya group. The broad westward movement is strongly supported, but the contributing source populations, corridors and number of migration pulses remain less certain [@haak_massive_2015; @papac_dynamic_2021; @ringbauer_accurate_2024].

### 2.3 Eastward movement into Inner Asia

Ancient DNA also supports an eastward expansion. @allentoft_population_2015 found Afanasievo individuals from the Altai^[A mountain region in Inner Asia where Russia, Mongolia, China and Kazakhstan meet.] to be genetically close to sampled Yamnaya groups, consistent with rapid movement across a very large distance in the early third millennium BCE. @wang_genomic_2021 extended this pattern into western Mongolia and Xinjiang, identifying Yamnaya/Afanasievo-related ancestry after approximately 3000 BCE. Their regional sequence shows that the ancestry later declined in parts of Mongolia while persisting farther west, demonstrating that eastward dispersal was followed by local admixture and population turnover^[A substantial change in a region’s population through migration, replacement or mixing.] rather than permanent demographic uniformity. @chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022 provide a broader chronological framework compatible with the formation and later spread of this ancestry.

The eastern evidence is less geographically continuous than the evidence from central Europe. Genetic similarity between Yamnaya and Afanasievo populations supports a broad eastward dispersal, but sparsely sampled intermediate areas limit reconstruction of the exact route. Archaeological labels also cannot substitute for ancestry: @wang_genomic_2021 report that an Afanasievo-associated context did not invariably correspond to Yamnaya-related genetic ancestry. The most defensible conclusion is therefore that closely related populations moved east toward the Altai, western Mongolia and Xinjiang after about 3000 BCE, while the detailed corridors and correspondence between archaeological and genetic classifications remain provisional [@allentoft_population_2015; @chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022; @wang_genomic_2021].

## 3. Routes, chronology and demographic consequences

### 3.1 A sequence rather than a single event

Across the evidence, Yamnaya-associated mobility is best understood as a sequence. Earlier mixtures in the Caucasus–Lower Volga, Dnipro–Don, North Pontic and southeastern European interaction zones supplied the ancestry and social connections from which expansion emerged. Direct target-period evidence then documents westward and eastward movement beginning around 3300–3000 BCE. Finally, regional studies record assimilation, further turnover and long-distance continuities during the later target period and after 2600 BCE [@chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022; @lazaridis_genetic_2025; @mathieson_genomic_2018; @nikitin_genomic_2025]. This sequence prevents later transformations—particularly Bell Beaker-period changes—from being projected backwards as direct evidence about Yamnaya communities.

The Corded Ware relationship illustrates both the strength and uncertainty of route reconstruction. Genome-wide ancestry and identity-by-descent evidence support rapid, recent genealogical connections with Yamnaya-related populations, but the sampled Yamnaya groups need not represent the only source. Corded Ware populations also incorporated ancestry related to earlier European groups and differed between regions. The data therefore favour substantial population movement followed by local admixture over either a purely cultural diffusion model or a uniform replacement by one genetically homogeneous migrant population [@haak_massive_2015; @papac_dynamic_2021; @ringbauer_accurate_2024].

### 3.2 Replacement, admixture and regional restructuring

Regional time series^[Genetic samples from the same region but from different periods, allowing researchers to track change over time.] show that the demographic consequences of Steppe migration varied markedly. In Bohemia, Corded Ware populations appeared by approximately 2900 BCE with high but variable Steppe-related ancestry, after which the incorporation of women with diverse ancestry and sharp changes in Y-chromosome lineages^[Lines of paternal descent traced through variants of the Y chromosome.] indicate repeated social and genetic restructuring. Some of the most pronounced changes occurred around 2600 BCE or later, so they represent the end of the target interval and its consequences rather than the initial Yamnaya expansion [@papac_dynamic_2021]. In southeastern Poland, genomic, kinship and strontium-isotope data^[Measurements of strontium in teeth that can help determine whether a person grew up locally or moved from another geological region.] instead reveal a smaller-scale pattern in which Steppe-associated paternal ancestry coexisted with maternal lineages^[Lines of descent traced through mothers, commonly studied using mitochondrial DNA.] related to earlier Neolithic populations, including kin relationships that crossed local and non-local mobility categories [@linderholm_corded_2020]. Together, these studies replace a single model of “mass migration” with evidence for multiple combinations of long-distance movement, local incorporation and community reorganisation.

The migration was often sex-biased^[A migration in which males and females participated in different proportions.], but its magnitude cannot be assumed to have been constant across Eurasia. @scorrano_genetic_2021 found stronger male bias in Steppe-related ancestry among several Corded Ware groups than among Bell Beaker groups, using autosomal^[Relating to the non-sex chromosomes, which are inherited from both parents.], X-chromosomal^[Relating to the X chromosome, whose inheritance pattern differs between males and females.] and uniparental comparisons. @linderholm_corded_2020 and @papac_dynamic_2021 likewise identify patterns consistent with male-linked Steppe ancestry and the incorporation of local or genetically diverse women. Nevertheless, these conclusions are best resolved in parts of central Europe and southeastern Poland, and some estimates are limited by small sample sizes, uneven genome coverage^[The proportion and depth of an ancient genome successfully recovered through DNA sequencing.] and low X-chromosome marker counts. Sex-biased mobility is thus a recurring regional mechanism, not a securely quantified Eurasia-wide constant [@linderholm_corded_2020; @papac_dynamic_2021; @scorrano_genetic_2021].

Later Bell Beaker evidence^[Evidence associated with the Bell Beaker phenomenon, named after its distinctive bell-shaped pottery.] further demonstrates why archaeological culture and population movement must be separated. @olalde_beaker_2018 found limited genetic affinity between Iberian and central European Beaker-associated groups, suggesting that some shared material practices spread without equivalent population movement. In Britain, by contrast, Beaker-associated migration introduced high Steppe-related ancestry and replaced approximately 90% of the existing gene pool^[The total collection of genetic variation present in a population.] within a few centuries. This British transformation mainly postdates 2600 BCE and is therefore a consequence of earlier Steppe-related dispersal rather than direct evidence for the initial Yamnaya migration. @tassi_genome_2017 provide a complementary earlier case: Globular Amphora^[A Late Neolithic archaeological culture of central and eastern Europe named after its rounded pottery vessels.] individuals in northwestern Poland were genetically closer to earlier Neolithic populations and lacked the expected Yamnaya-derived profile despite eastern archaeological affinities. Taken together, these results show that material culture can spread through cultural transmission in one context and accompany major demographic change in another [@olalde_beaker_2018; @tassi_genome_2017].

## 4. Migration and Indo-European language dispersal

### 4.1 A compatible demographic mechanism

The scale and speed of Yamnaya-related movement provide a credible demographic mechanism through which languages could have dispersed. @haak_massive_2015 interpreted the major Steppe-derived ancestry influx into central Europe as support for a Steppe-origin model for at least some Indo-European languages, while explicitly acknowledging that genetic data are silent about the language spoken by sampled individuals. @allentoft_population_2015 similarly described the bidirectional genomic transformations of Bronze Age Eurasia as consistent with a proposed early Bronze Age dispersal of Indo-European languages. These conclusions are meaningful because large movements of people create opportunities for language transmission, but they do not demonstrate that population replacement and language replacement occurred at the same rate or through the same social process.

The reviewed studies vary in how directly they discuss language. Some make explicit linguistic interpretations of their demographic results, whereas others supply indirect evidence about migration chronology, scale, sex bias or social incorporation. The latter studies should not be presented as independent confirmation of a linguistic hypothesis. For example, identity-by-descent links between Yamnaya and Corded Ware groups strengthen the evidence for recent population movement, but do not identify the language of either group [@ringbauer_accurate_2024]. Likewise, sex-biased ancestry and kinship structures may help reconstruct how migrants were incorporated, but they cannot show which languages were used within households or transmitted to later generations [@linderholm_corded_2020; @papac_dynamic_2021; @scorrano_genetic_2021].

### 4.2 Eastward dispersal and the proto-Tocharian interpretation

The eastward Yamnaya–Afanasievo connection has particular relevance to proposals concerning proto-Tocharian^[The reconstructed ancestor of the extinct Tocharian languages once spoken in parts of the Tarim Basin.]. @wang_genomic_2021 argue that the movement of a population closely related to Yamnaya into the Altai and farther into Inner Asia adds weight to a migration-mediated account of proto-Tocharian dispersal. @allentoft_population_2015 and @chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022 provide supporting demographic and chronological context for this eastward movement. However, “proto-Tocharian” is a linguistic interpretation applied to the demographic pattern, not a genetic measurement. Sparse sampling along intermediate routes and the imperfect correspondence between Afanasievo archaeological contexts and Yamnaya-related ancestry make a one-to-one mapping between population movement and language branch unjustified [@allentoft_population_2015; @chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022; @wang_genomic_2021].

Broader proposals about Indo-European roots require the same caution. @lazaridis_genetic_2025 connect their reconstruction of Caucasus–Lower Volga and North Pontic ancestry formation to a model of proto-Indo-Anatolian unity^[A proposed ancestral stage before the Anatolian languages separated from the other Indo-European branches.] before Yamnaya expansion and later language branching. This is the collection’s most explicit integration of genetic, archaeological and linguistic reasoning, but the linguistic conclusion remains dependent on the demographic model and independent linguistic assumptions. The unresolved location of some source populations and routes, including proposed connections towards Anatolia, prevents genetic models alone from determining a language homeland. @tassi_genome_2017 reinforce this limitation from the opposite direction: an archaeological group can display eastern cultural affinities without the expected Steppe ancestry, and language change need not follow demographic movement exactly. Genetic evidence can therefore test whether a proposed language-spread model has a plausible population mechanism, but it cannot adjudicate language identity by itself [@lazaridis_genetic_2025; @tassi_genome_2017].

## 5. Limits of linking genes, archaeological culture and language

The broad directions of Yamnaya-related movement are more secure than their fine-grained routes. Ancient-DNA models depend on the populations available as ancestry proxies^[Sampled populations used as stand-ins when estimating the ancestry of another population.], and unsampled groups may have contributed to both Yamnaya and Corded Ware populations. Admixture-date methods can also compress several closely spaced movements into an approximate date, while identity-by-descent detection depends on genome coverage and performs most reliably for longer segments. These constraints do not overturn the evidence for rapid dispersal, but they limit claims about a single point of origin, a unique migration corridor or an exact number of pulses^[Separate episodes or waves of migration.] [@chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022; @lazaridis_genetic_2025; @nikitin_genomic_2025; @ringbauer_accurate_2024].

The evidence is geographically and chronologically uneven. Central and northern Europe contain comparatively dense regional and community-level datasets, whereas the lower Volga, North Pontic–Caucasus zones, northern Eurasia and intermediate Inner Asian corridors remain less continuously sampled. Research using modern northern Eurasian genomes and published ancient comparators provides context for older Siberian–European interactions, but cannot substitute for a direct transect^[A sequence of samples collected across a geographic route or a series of locations.] of Yamnaya-period individuals [@wong_reconstructing_2017]. Similarly, studies spanning millennia must isolate the 3300–2600 BCE evidence from earlier ancestry formation and later Bronze Age consequences. Without this separation, later replacement or modern-population affinity can be mistaken for direct evidence about Yamnaya migration [@chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022; @mathieson_genomic_2018; @olalde_beaker_2018; @wong_reconstructing_2017].

Most importantly, ancestry, archaeological culture, ethnicity and language are distinct analytical categories. An individual may be buried in a Corded Ware or Afanasievo context without possessing a uniform ancestry profile, and a population may adopt material practices without large-scale genetic change. Conversely, a substantial ancestry shift demonstrates migration but does not reveal whether incoming languages replaced, coexisted with or were adopted by local populations. None of the genetic studies reviewed contains a direct linguistic dataset capable of testing speech, branching, borrowing or multilingualism. Ancient DNA can therefore support or constrain demographic scenarios associated with Indo-European dispersal, but the linguistic argument ultimately requires independent historical-linguistic and archaeological evidence [@tassi_genome_2017; @wang_genomic_2021].

## 6. Synthesis and research gaps

Ancient DNA provides strong evidence that Yamnaya-related mobility was a major Eurasian demographic process during 3300–2600 BCE. The most coherent reconstruction is a multi-stage formation process involving interaction among Caucasus–Lower Volga-related, Dnipro–Don/North Pontic and neighbouring populations, followed by rapid expansion from approximately 3300 BCE. Westward movement into central and northern Europe is supported by large ancestry shifts and recent genealogical links, while the genetic relationship between Yamnaya and Afanasievo populations supports a parallel eastward movement towards the Altai and Inner Asia. In both directions, migration was followed by regionally different mixtures of incorporation, sex bias, continuity and replacement rather than a single uniform process [@allentoft_population_2015; @haak_massive_2015; @lazaridis_genetic_2025; @nikitin_genomic_2025; @papac_dynamic_2021; @ringbauer_accurate_2024; @wang_genomic_2021].

Several questions remain unresolved. Direct sampling is still insufficient to define every lower-Volga, North Pontic, Caucasus or possible Anatolian route, and intermediate populations between the Pontic–Caspian Steppe and Inner Asia remain sparse. Source substructure^[Genetic differences among smaller groups within what might otherwise be treated as one source population.] and chronological resolution^[How precisely the available evidence can distinguish events occurring at different times.] make it difficult to distinguish one large migration from several closely spaced movements. Community-level studies of kinship, mobility and sex bias are concentrated in a limited number of European settings, restricting comparison across Eurasia. More matched archaeological–genetic transects are needed to determine when similar material cultures reflect population movement, local adoption or mixed processes [@chintalapati_spatiotemporal_2022; @lazaridis_genetic_2025; @linderholm_corded_2020; @nikitin_genomic_2025; @papac_dynamic_2021; @wang_genomic_2021].

The largest interpretive gap concerns language. The demographic expansion is compatible with some Steppe-based models of Indo-European dispersal and supplies a plausible mechanism for moving languages across large distances. It does not, however, establish the speech of Yamnaya, Corded Ware or Afanasievo individuals, nor does it independently resolve language homelands, branches or transmission mechanisms. The defensible conclusion is therefore two-part: ancient DNA strongly supports rapid bidirectional dispersal of Yamnaya-related populations and subsequent regional restructuring, while any connection between those movements and particular Indo-European languages remains an interdisciplinary inference rather than a direct genetic finding [@haak_massive_2015; @lazaridis_genetic_2025; @tassi_genome_2017; @wang_genomic_2021].
